classification.difficultyReason: Cubic expansion and grouping with the assumption for divisibility by 3, as in the reference.

children.label: a
children.prompt: $n^3+8n$ is divisible by $3$ for all integers $n\geq1$.

answer.short: $(k+1)^3+8(k+1)=3(p+k^2+k+3)$, using $k^3+8k=3p$. The base case is true, so the result holds for all integers $n\geq1$ by induction.
answer.worked:
Test $n=1$
$$\mathrm{LHS}=1^3+8(1)=9=3(3)$$
$\therefore$ True for $n=1$

Assume true for $n=k$
$k^3+8k=3p$, where $p$ is an integer.

Prove $n=k+1$
WTP: $(k+1)^3+8(k+1)=3q$, where $q$ is an integer.
$$\begin{align*}\mathrm{LHS}&=(k+1)^3+8(k+1)\\&=k^3+3k^2+3k+1+8k+8\\&=(k^3+8k)+3k^2+3k+9\\&=3p+3k^2+3k+9\quad\text{using assumption}\\&=3(p+k^2+k+3)\\&=3q\end{align*}$$
Since $p$ and $k$ are integers, $q=p+k^2+k+3$ is also an integer.

Since true for $n=1$ and truth for $n=k$ implies truth for $n=k+1$, it is true for all integers $n\geq1$ by mathematical induction.

children.label: b
children.prompt: $2n^3+n$ is divisible by $3$ for all integers $n\geq1$.

answer.short: $2(k+1)^3+(k+1)=3(p+2k^2+2k+1)$, using $2k^3+k=3p$. The base case is true, so the result holds for all integers $n\geq1$ by induction.
answer.worked:
Test $n=1$
$$\mathrm{LHS}=2(1)^3+1=3$$
$\therefore$ True for $n=1$

Assume true for $n=k$
$2k^3+k=3p$, where $p$ is an integer.

Prove $n=k+1$
WTP: $2(k+1)^3+(k+1)=3q$, where $q$ is an integer.
$$\begin{align*}\mathrm{LHS}&=2(k+1)^3+(k+1)\\&=2k^3+6k^2+6k+2+k+1\\&=(2k^3+k)+6k^2+6k+3\\&=3p+6k^2+6k+3\quad\text{using assumption}\\&=3(p+2k^2+2k+1)\\&=3q\end{align*}$$
Since $p$ and $k$ are integers, $q=p+2k^2+2k+1$ is also an integer.

Since true for $n=1$ and truth for $n=k$ implies truth for $n=k+1$, it is true for all integers $n\geq1$ by mathematical induction.
